turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Morning, Mr Hale. Come through and sit yourself down. The nurse has already jotted a few numbers, but I'd rather start with you.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, Doctor. I'm sorry to take the time. It's been a rather trying week, and not only because of the rain.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): The rain can wait. What's been troubling you?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, when I rise from the armchair I go light-headed. Not a spinning sensation, more a draining feeling, and twice I have...
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Twice you have?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Slid down. I must be precise. I did not fall. My daughter is fond of the word fall, and I do think it overstates the matter. I lowered myself to the carpet.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): She had a word with reception. She said you fell twice this week and that you tend to make light of it.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): She does worry, bless her. Sunday, in the hallway, and yesterday beside the kitchen table. I sat, rather than dropped. No bruise, no cut, nothing of that sort.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Did you black out at any point? Even for a second?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I was entirely aware. A little foolish, if I'm honest, but conscious throughout.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): And this light-headed feeling — is it every time you stand?

[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Not every time. Most mornings, and if I get up quickly when the news finishes. It eases if I keep a hand on the chair. Um, the bus was late today, which is neither here nor there.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long has the light-headedness been going on? Can you date the first time you slid?

[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): The light-headedness, oh, a few weeks. The sliding... I cannot give you a tidy date for when it began. Sunday was one, and yesterday the other. Before that I only felt odd.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain with these episodes? Palpitations? Breathlessness?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain. No pounding in the chest. I wouldn't say breathless. I am more tired than I was, particularly...
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, I talked over you. Tired particularly when?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): In the afternoons. I have put it down to sleeping poorly, which is the reason for the night tablet.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll list the tablets in a moment. Nausea? Headache? Any change in the waterworks?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No nausea. No headache to speak of. The waterworks are much as they have always been, nothing new.

[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Before you came in, the nurse took lying and standing pressures. Lying, one hundred and fifty-two over eighty-eight. Standing, one hundred and six over sixty-four. Pulse seventy-six when you were lying.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Forgive me, I don't wish to be difficult. I heard her say one hundred and forty over eighty for the lying reading. I was paying attention.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Then we have a disagreement to record. The chart says one fifty-two over eighty-eight lying, standing one oh six over sixty-four. You recall one forty over eighty lying.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. I may have misheard, of course. I can only tell you what I believe she said.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Quite. Medicines next. You're on treatment for the blood pressure, and something to help you sleep?

[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): That is correct. Amlodipine five milligrams in the morning. Ramipril five milligrams, morning as well. Bendroflumethiazide, two point five milligrams I think, with breakfast. And zopiclone three point seven five at night.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): You sounded unsure about the bendroflumethiazide.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): The packet does say two point five. I hesitate because the chemist once queried the strength. I am reasonably sure that is what I take.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll go with two point five milligrams for now. Do you take the zopiclone every night, as it was prescribed?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No. About four nights a week. I dislike depending on it, so I leave it off when I can.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you stopped anything, or been given a medicine you never actually started?

[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): I stopped the simvastatin in March. My legs ached. And after the last appointment there was a prescription for doxazosin — I never took a single one. It felt like one tablet too many.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): So simvastatin stopped since March, doxazosin never started. Any drug allergies?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): None that I am aware of.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll examine you quickly. Heart sounds are regular, and I don't hear a murmur. The chest is clear. No swelling at the ankles. Sitting here, you look steady.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): That is reassuring. My daughter had rather talked herself into something grave.

[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me think aloud for a moment. A fall in pressure on standing would fit the light-headedness and the sliding, and three blood pressure tablets can do that. It could instead be the inner ear, or a rhythm problem I can't pick up by listening. I'm not calling this a stroke, and I won't lock in a diagnosis before the tests.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): So you are not certain it is the tablets?
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): My working impression is a postural drop from the blood pressure treatment. I can't exclude a heart rhythm disturbance. I don't want to go further than that today.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Then what would you like to change? I should prefer not to alter everything at once.

[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Only one tablet. You're taking ramipril five milligrams; from tomorrow, please take two point five milligrams each morning. Leave the amlodipine and the bendroflumethiazide as they are.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Ramipril down to two point five. Yes, I can do that. And the zopiclone?

[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Keep the zopiclone at three point seven five, and only on the nights you need it. When you get up, sit on the edge of the bed first, then stand. If the light-headedness comes, sit down at once. Please don't drive while you're dizzy.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): I have not driven this week, as it happens. I shall be careful on the stairs at home.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'd like an ECG today, and a blood test for kidney function and electrolytes, because we're changing the ramipril. The nurse can do both before you go.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Today is perfectly convenient.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the dizziness gets worse, or you black out, or you develop chest pain, don't wait for me — go to A&E the same day.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand, and I shall tell my daughter the same.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Otherwise I'll see you here in two weeks, with those results, and we'll see whether the lower dose has helped.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks. Thank you, Doctor. You have been very clear, which I do appreciate.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bring the bendroflumethiazide box next time, so we can settle that strength. Mind how you go.

spec.situation: Older patient who fell twice 'but not really fell, slid down'; dizzy on standing; takes several BP and sleeping tablets; daughter reports what the patient minimises; nurse reads lying and standing BP; doctor changes one tablet.
features: interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.

stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.

doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.
disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.

omissions.text: Patient explicitly said the episodes were not falls: he 'slid down'/'lowered myself to the carpet' and remained conscious throughout; daughter described them as falls but patient disputed that wording.
No bruises or cuts after the two sliding episodes.
Dizziness is not vertigo: patient described light-headedness as 'not a spinning sensation, more a draining feeling.'
Amlodipine and bendroflumethiazide were specifically to be left unchanged when ramipril was reduced.
Doctor also considered an inner ear cause in the differential.
Doctor stated he was not calling this a stroke and would not lock in a diagnosis before tests.
ECG and blood tests were to be done before the patient left today by the nurse.
Follow-up plan was to review the results in two weeks and assess whether the lower ramipril dose had helped.
